title: agentskills/agentskills — Specification and documentation for Agent Skills
content:
A standardized way to give AI agents new capabilities and expertise.
Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows.
At its core, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file. This file includes metadata (name and description, at minimum) and instructions that tell an agent how to perform a specific task. Skills can also bundle scripts, reference materials, templates, and other resources.
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md          # Required: metadata + instructions
├── scripts/          # Optional: executable code
├── references/       # Optional: documentation
├── assets/           # Optional: templates, resources
└── ...               # Any additional files or directories
Agents are increasingly capable, but often don't have the context they need to do real work reliably. Skills solve this by packaging procedural knowledge and company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders that agents load on demand. This gives agents:
- Domain expertise: Capture specialized knowledge — from legal review processes to data analysis pipelines to presentation formatting — as reusable instructions and resources.
- Repeatable workflows: Turn multi-step tasks into consistent, auditable procedures.
- Cross-product reuse: Build a skill once and use it across any skills-compatible agent.
Agents load skills through progressive disclosure, in three stages:
- Discovery: At startup, agents load only the name and description of each available skill, just enough to know when it might be relevant.
- Activation: When a task matches a skill's description, the agent reads the full SKILL.md instructions into context.
- Execution: The agent follows the instructions, optionally executing bundled code or loading referenced files as needed.
Full instructions load only when a task calls for them, so agents can keep many skills on hand with only a small context footprint.
Agent Skills are supported by a large number of AI tools and agentic clients — see the Client Showcase to explore some of them!
- Documentation — Guides and tutorials
- Specification — Format details
- Example Skills — See what's possible
- Discord — Share what you're building!
The Agent Skills format was originally developed by Anthropic, released as an open standard, and has been adopted by a growing number of agent products. The standard is open to contributions from the broader ecosystem — see CONTRIBUTING.md for how to get involved.
Code in this repository is licensed under Apache 2.0. Documentation is licensed under CC-BY-4.0. See individual directories for details.

report.summary: Agent Skills is an open, lightweight format that packages procedural knowledge and context into portable SKILL.md folders, letting AI agents load specialized capabilities on demand.
report.background: As agents grew more capable, a gap emerged: models could call tools but often lacked the private, procedural context needed to do real work reliably. Teams compensated with long system prompts, retrieval hacks, or bespoke plugins, none of which traveled between products. Anthropic originally developed the Agent Skills format and released it as an open standard, following the pattern set by MCP for tool connectivity — standardize the packaging, let the ecosystem build on it. The repository now hosts the specification, documentation, and example skills, with adoption spreading across agentic clients. Code is Apache 2.0, documentation CC-BY-4.0, and contributions are open to the broader ecosystem.
key_points: A skill is just a folder containing a required SKILL.md file with at minimum a name, a description, and instructions. Optional subfolders can bundle executable scripts, reference documentation, templates, and other assets, so procedural knowledge ships as a version-controlled artifact rather than a fragile prompt blob.

Progressive disclosure is the core design trick. Agents load only skill names and descriptions at startup, pull full instructions into context when a task matches, and load bundled files or run code only at execution time — letting an agent keep dozens of skills available at minimal context cost.

Skills target three problems: domain expertise (legal review, data pipelines, deck formatting), repeatable multi-step workflows that become auditable, and cross-product reuse so one skill works across any compatible agent client rather than a single vendor.

The format was originated by Anthropic and released as an open standard with permissive licensing (Apache 2.0 for code, CC-BY-4.0 for docs). A client showcase and example skill library exist, and the spec accepts outside contributions — an explicit bid to avoid single-vendor lock-in.

Skills are complementary to tool protocols rather than competing: tools define what an agent can call, skills define how and when to do a job. The two layers together form a rough stack of capability plus competence for agentic systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Agent Skills gives agent builders a shared packaging unit, which lowers switching costs and shifts competition toward skill quality and curation rather than proprietary plumbing. For developers, it means reusable, testable, version-controlled expertise — write once, run in any compatible client, review changes in a diff like normal code. The risk is fragmentation if large vendors extend the format incompatibly, or if skill marketplaces fill with low-quality, unvetted instructions that quietly steer agents wrong. For regular users, the payoff is agents that actually know their team's processes and formats, with more predictable behavior and less re-explaining — though provenance and security of third-party skills will become a real concern.
report.tools: Start with the agentskills/agentskills repo for the specification, docs, and example skills, then read the Client Showcase to find compatible agents. Anthropic's Claude Code and Agent SDK are natural places to try authoring a SKILL.md. Pair skills with MCP for tool access, keep skills in git for review, and test progressive disclosure by watching context usage as your skill library grows.
